claims.text: Tailored thermal annealing can promote short-range order in a high-entropy alloy.
Rapid quenching can retain a random solid solution with negligible short-range order.
There is a sub-melting thermal-treatment regime in which atomic mobility permits SRO development without precipitation or long-range ordering.
Diffuse scattering or atom probe tomography can quantify the extent and nature of local chemical ordering.
Short-range order is associated with increased stacking-fault energy in FCC multi-principal-element alloys.
Higher stacking-fault energy makes the motion of leading partial dislocations encounter greater resistance and a higher energy barrier.
Passage of a trailing partial can erase the stacking fault and restore the FCC structure.
A trailing partial moving through an SRO-containing slip plane creates a diffuse antiphase boundary by destroying the local order.
The energy penalty associated with stacking-fault creation and antiphase-boundary generation produces back-stress that retards dislocation motion.
SRO-mediated retardation of dislocation motion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Increasing SRO through thermal treatment will increase yield strength relative to a quenched random-solid-solution baseline.
Increasing SRO through thermal treatment will increase hardness relative to a quenched random-solid-solution baseline.
Greater SRO should correlate with greater resistance to dislocation motion.
The proposed SRO mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys in which precipitation and long-range ordering do not occur.
Grain-size-dependent Hall–Petch strengthening can also govern alloy strength and can confound attribution of strength changes to SRO.
The SRO mechanism may cease to govern behavior when grain-boundary-mediated plasticity dominates.
The SRO mechanism may cease to govern behavior when precipitate strengthening dominates.
Annealing-induced grain growth is a potential competing effect that must be separated from SRO strengthening.
